rationale: B wins because it stares at the kill question and makes a usable angle out of it: “Deel's AI will flag whether your contractor is really an employee. It won't say how often it's wrong.” A is strong, but “an AI that makes that call across 150 countries” turns a risk-flagging tool into a legal decision-maker, which is how you buy yourself a correction. Both sets understand the lawsuit is background radiation, not the pitch; B is just cleaner about what can be defended this week.
gaps_in_A: “an AI that makes that call across 150 countries” overstates the supplied fact. The update says the tool flags risks; it does not say the AI decides classification.
“tracks all 150 in real time” is not in the update. Maintenance cadence and real-time legal updating are exactly the facts a trade reporter would demand, not facts to smuggle into the angle.

“raises the cost of competing on compliance as a standalone offering” is plausible market analysis, but the update gives no competitor/product map. A correctly asks for proof, but the headline still leans on an unproven lock-in thesis.
gaps_in_B: “One employer, one bad contractor call” is useful only as a conditional assignment. With no named customer, jurisdiction, or actual flag supplied, it should be framed more explicitly as a bring-me-proof angle, not a kept story.

“when the tool clears a worker a labor inspector later reclassifies” invents product behavior. The update says the tool flags risks; it does not say it clears workers or issues pass/fail determinations.
“funding-mechanics” is the wrong label for the pricing angle. The substance is AI monetization or bundling strategy; sloppy taxonomy is not fatal, but it makes the angle look less newsroom-native.
“150 jurisdictions” quietly swaps the supplied “150 countries.” In labor law, that distinction matters. Legal-compliance reporters notice this stuff.
